info.text: Quiz: 20 questions (multiple choice, code tracing, drag and drop).

questiontext.text: What should you do first when you meet a simulation problem?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A simulation is only as good as your understanding of the rules. Once the state variables are clear, the code is usually a short loop.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Read the rules carefully and decide which variables describe the state
Write the loop immediately and fix it later
Look for a formula that skips the process

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int people = 0, best = 0;
int out[] = {0, 3, 2};
int in[]  = {4, 5, 1};
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    people = people - out[i] + in[i];
    best = max(best, people);
}
cout << best << " " << people << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The bus holds 4, then 4 - 3 + 5 = 6, then 6 - 2 + 1 = 5 people. The largest value ever reached is 6, while the final count is 5.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Directions are numbered 0 = north, 1 = east, 2 = south, 3 = west. Which formula turns right?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Turning right moves to the next direction, and the remainder brings west (3) back to north (0). Turning left is (d + 3) % 4, which avoids a negative number.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
const int dx[4] = {0, 1, 0, -1};
const int dy[4] = {-1, 0, 1, 0};
int x = 0, y = 0, d = 1;
for (char c : string("FFRF")) {
    if (c == 'R') {
        d = (d + 1) % 4;
    } else if (c == 'L') {
        d = (d + 3) % 4;
    } else {
        x += dx[d];
        y += dy[d];
    }
}
cout << x << " " << y << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The robot starts facing east (d = 1). Two steps forward reach (2, 0). R turns it to face south (d = 2), and the last F moves it down one row to (2, 1).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which statement about a queue is correct?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A queue is "first in, first out". The container with "last in, first out" is the stack.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: The first element added is the first one removed
The last element added is the first one removed
It allows access by index such as q[2]

name.text: Q07 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct command into the gap so the program prints 2 (the front child goes to the back of the line, then the new front is printed).

main.cpp
queue<int> q;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    q.push(i);
}
q.push(q.front());
q.[[1]]();
cout << q.front() << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. After push(q.front()) the queue is 1 2 3 4 1. Removing the old front with pop leaves 2 3 4 1, so the new front is 2.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
queue<int> q;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    q.push(i);
}
q.push(q.front());
q.pop();
cout << q.front() << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each simulation term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

State  →  [[1]]

Generation  →  [[2]]

Queue  →  [[3]]

Cycle  →  [[4]]

Boundary check  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Most simulation bugs come from one of these five ideas, so they are worth knowing by name.

The correct answer:

  • State → The variables that describe the current situation
  • Generation → The grid after one full step of the Game of Life
  • Queue → First in, first out container
  • Cycle → A series of states that repeats
  • Boundary check → Making sure a position is inside the grid

questiontext.text:
Sort each situation: is a queue or a set the better tool?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Children counting around a circle  →  [[1]]

Detecting that a number sequence repeats a value  →  [[2]]

A first come, first served line  →  [[1]]

Remembering which grid cells a robot visited  →  [[2]]

Moving people from the front to the back  →  [[1]]

Checking whether a state was seen before  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A queue models order of service and rotation. A set answers "have I seen this before?" quickly, which is exactly what cycle detection and visited cells need.

The correct answer:

queue: Children counting around a circle, A first come, first served line, Moving people from the front to the back
set: Detecting that a number sequence repeats a value, Remembering which grid cells a robot visited, Checking whether a state was seen before

questiontext.text: Why does the Game of Life build the next generation in a new grid?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Every cell must be judged using the old generation. Writing the results into a separate grid keeps the old values intact until the whole step is finished.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Changing the current grid while counting would corrupt the neighbor counts of cells not yet processed
To use more memory on purpose
Because a grid cannot be modified
To make the cells die faster

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int n = 19, steps = 0;
while (n != 1) {
    int s = 0;
    for (int t = n; t > 0; t /= 10) {
        s += (t % 10) * (t % 10);
    }
    n = s;
    steps++;
}
cout << steps << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The sequence is 19 → 82 → 68 → 100 → 1. That is four applications of the rule before the number reaches 1.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: A problem asks for the state after 10¹² steps of a process that repeats. What is the usual idea?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. If states repeat, the process becomes periodic. Detect the first repeated state (for example with a set), and use % cycle_length to skip the repetition.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Find the cycle, then use the remainder to jump ahead
Use a bigger integer type only

questiontext.text: Which queue command removes the element at the front?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. pop deletes the front element (it returns nothing). front only reads it, and push adds a new element at the back.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
queue<int> q;
for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
    q.push(i);
}
while (!q.empty()) {
    q.push(q.front());
    q.pop();
    cout << q.front() << " ";
    q.pop();
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Every round skips one child (moving it to the back) and removes the next one. The removal order is 2, 4, 3 and finally 1: this is the circle game with k = 2.

name.text: Q16 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct operator into the gap so the robot is stopped by the wall (it should print bump).

main.cpp
int W = 3, x = 2, nx = x + 1;
if (nx >= 0 && nx [[1]] W) {
    cout << "move" << endl;
} else {
    cout << "bump" << endl;
}

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Valid columns are 0 to W - 1, so the new column must be strictly smaller than W. With <= the robot would wrongly step outside the board.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int W = 3, x = 2, nx = x + 1;
if (nx >= 0 && nx < W) {
    cout << "move" << endl;
} else {
    cout << "bump" << endl;
}

questiontext.text:
Arrange the steps that compute one generation of the Game of Life.

Drag the steps into the correct order.

1. [[1]]

2. [[2]]

3. [[3]]

4. [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The new grid protects the old values while the neighbors are counted. Only after all cells are decided do we swap the grids.

The correct answer:

  1. Create an empty grid for the next generation
  2. For each cell, count its live neighbors in the current grid
  3. Decide alive or dead with the rules and store it in the new grid
  4. Replace the current grid with the new grid

questiontext.text:
Match each code idea with its purpose.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

dx[d] and dy[d]  →  [[1]]

(d + 1) % 4  →  [[2]]

(d + 3) % 4  →  [[3]]

set of visited states  →  [[4]]

q.push(q.front()); q.pop();  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These small patterns appear again and again in robot, board and circle simulations.

The correct answer:

  • dx[d] and dy[d] → How far to move in direction d
  • (d + 1) % 4 → Turn right
  • (d + 3) % 4 → Turn left
  • set of visited states → Detect a cycle or count distinct cells
  • q.push(q.front()); q.pop(); → Move the front element to the back

questiontext.text:
Sort each habit: good practice or common mistake in simulation?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

Editing the grid while counting neighbors  →  [[2]]

Building the next generation in a copy  →  [[1]]

Skipping the boundary check  →  [[2]]

Testing a tiny example by hand  →  [[1]]

Forgetting that the start cell counts as visited  →  [[2]]

Storing visited states in a set  →  [[1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Most simulation bugs come from corrupting the state while reading it, leaving the board, or forgetting the starting situation. Small hand-made tests and visited sets protect you.

The correct answer:

Good practice: Building the next generation in a copy, Testing a tiny example by hand, Storing visited states in a set
Common mistake: Editing the grid while counting neighbors, Skipping the boundary check, Forgetting that the start cell counts as visited

questiontext.text: In the bus problem (maximum number of passengers), where should best be updated?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The bus may be at its fullest in the middle of the trip. Updating after each stop catches that moment, while the final count would miss it.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Inside the loop, after every stop
